output.brief: The evidence doesn't support the claim that proximity bias explains the gap. Only 32% of remote staff have the 18 months in level that the promotion policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people, nomination, approval and promotion rates are nearly the same: 20.0% remote vs 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote group's eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, and the observed rate is 7.6%. The remote group is mostly newer hires, which is consistent with the manager's comment that his remote staff haven't been with the company long. The remaining 1.1-point difference rests on 110 people and could be chance. Don't confirm proximity bias, and don't announce the three-day office rule. It would penalise about 180 people hired on home-based contracts for a gap that is mostly about tenure. I could not test whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments, because the staffing system doesn't record it. I also didn't check whether remote staff leave at higher rates or why more remote staff are recent hires. Next steps: put the rule on hold, report promotion rates for eligible staff only, and re-check at FY2027. Meanwhile, start collecting data on who gets stretch work. Confidence is fairly high on the main finding and low on the secondary questions.
